name: Compare how security is organised in small, medium-sized and large companies. What are the pros and cons of each, and when do companies usually start taking security seriously?
answer: Small company: typically no security team – a one-man show (sometimes not even that); security is a function of the IT team or admin, perceived as not important, mostly about backup and authentication. Pro: at least one person who understands security. Con: knowledge and experience of just one person. Medium-sized company: a small all-purpose team dealing with operational, infrastructure and application layers, but nobody knows everything; security is seen as an unnecessary evil (maybe until a breach). Pro: a dedicated security team. Cons: budget, limited experience with various aspects of security. Big company: big dedicated team(s), not all focused on security (e.g. a privacy team), each focused on a different area – security architecture, engineering, SOC, application security, consulting, pentesting, CISO. Pros: dedicated teams, detailed experience, possibly a dedicated budget. Cons: security costs a lot, slower innovation. Companies usually start taking security seriously only after a major incident or an audit; before that there is minimal budget, minimal people and minimal respect for security (“why should we be a target”). The Uber example shows that security budgets often grow only after an incident.
keyPoints: Small: no team, IT admin, backup and authentication; one person's knowledge
Medium: small all-purpose team, unnecessary evil, budget limits
Large: dedicated specialised teams and budget, but expensive and slower innovation
Typical subteams: architecture, engineering, SOC, AppSec, pentesting, consulting, CISO
Seriousness usually comes after an incident or audit

name: Describe the SolarWinds attack: the vector, the targets, the actor's traits, and what it teaches about security operations.
answer: SolarWinds is a software company making network management products; its popular product Orion was used by governments and major corporations and approved for sensitive areas. The attacker (UNC2452, publicly revealed by FireEye) accessed SolarWinds in 2019, injected test code and then the SUNBURST malware into Orion builds; the compromised update was shipped to customers in 2020. Customers who carefully kept Orion patched and updated installed it – about 18,000 companies, government agencies, think tanks, universities and NGOs. SUNBURST waited about 14 days, then went live only at a handful of high-value targets and stayed asleep everywhere else. The actor was very sophisticated: cleaned up trace evidence, had good security on its own servers, hid its servers and exploit. The motivation was murky – limited target selection, no financial interest, no DoS, no data destruction or ransomware, no personal information theft. Lesson: it was a supply-chain attack through malicious software updates – even careful customers who kept Orion patched were hit, because the trusted supplier's update itself was compromised.
keyPoints: Vector: malicious SUNBURST code in SolarWinds Orion updates (supply chain)
~18,000 installations; activated only at a handful of valuable targets after ~14 days
Very sophisticated actor: cleaned traces, hid servers and exploit
Murky motivation: no financial interest, no ransomware, no data destruction
Lesson: a compromised supplier update hits even well-patched customers
